etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin addictus, past participle of addīcō (“deliver; devote; surrender”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + dīcō (“say; declare”)

definitions.definition: A person who is addicted, especially to a harmful drug.

quote.citation: 2006 June 25, Benoit Denizet-Lewis, “An Anti-Addiction Pill?”, in The New York Times Magazine‎[1]:
quote.text: Those nonaddicts who picked a winning card had increased blood flow to the striatum, but the gambling addicts who picked the right card had much less of it (their reward system was less active).

quote.citation: 2011 August 1, Richard A. Friedman, “Who Falls to Addiction, and Who Is Unscathed?”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: A stressful environment in which there is ready access to drugs can trump a low genetic risk of addiction in these animals. The same may be true for humans, too. And that’s a notion many find hard to believe: Just about anyone, regardless of baseline genetic risk, can become an addict under the right circumstances.

definitions.definition: (transitive, Ancient Rome) To deliver (someone or something) following a judicial decision. [from 16th c.]
(reflexive, now rare, archaic) To devote (oneself) to a given activity, occupation, thing etc. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1640–1706, John Evelyn, “(please specify the date of the diary entry)”, in William Bray, editor, Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn, […], 2nd edition, volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […]; and sold by John and Arthur Arch, […], published 1819, →OCLC:
quote.text: They addict themselves to the civil law.

quote.citation: 1751, [Tobias] Smollett, chapter 88, in The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle […], volume III, London: Harrison and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Having resided some time in this place, we returned to the other country-house which we had left, where lord B— addicted himself so much to hunting, and other male diversions, that I began to think he neglected me  […] .

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To bind (a person or thing) to the service of something. [16th–18th c.]
(reflexive, obsolete) To devote or pledge (oneself) to a given person, cause etc. [16th–19th c.]
(transitive, now rare, archaic) To devote (one's mind, talent etc.) to a given activity, occupation, thing etc. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: January 19, 1754, Samuel Johnson, The Adventurer, number 126:
quote.text: That part of mankind that addict their minds to speculations.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make (someone) become devoted to a given thing or activity; to cause to be addicted. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: a. 1662 (date written), Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England, London:  […]  J[ohn] G[rismond,] W[illiam] L[eybourne] and W[illiam] G[odbid], published 1662, →OCLC:
quote.text: His genius addicted him to the study of antiquity.
